paper_title: Regret Bounds for Robust Online Decision Making
source_locator: Explicit open question on PDF page 4
statement: We apply our methods to derive upper bounds on regret in two special cases. One case is tabular episodic robust online reinforcement learning, a generalization of which was studied in Tian et al. (2021). The motivation of Tian et al. (2021) was studying multi-agent learning, but since an RMDP can be rephrased as a zero-sum two-player stochastic 4 √ game , their results apply to our framework. There, we get a regret bound of Õ(H S 3 AT ), where H is the episode length, S is the number of states, A is the number of actions, and T is the number of√episodes. For T ≫ 0, this is an improvement on Tian et al. 3 (2021)’s bound of Õ(H 2 SAT 2 ). However, our algorithm is not computationally efficient. It remains an open√question whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm with regret of Õ(poly(H, S, A) T )5 .
context: In Foster et al. (2023), the algorithm that implements that upper bound requires access to an online distribution learning oracle, and the bound scales with the statistical complexity of the latter. This statistical complexity has bounds in terms of model class cardinality or covering number, which are derived in Foster et al. (2021) using the techniques of Vovk (1995). In our setting, we require a similar oracle for robust online distribution learning. Again, we derive similar bounds on statistical complexity, but this requires different techniques: our algorithm imitates a prediction market, an idea inspired by Shafer et al. Notation and General Framework Lambda notation for functions is used throughout. ∆X is the space of probability distributions on a space X. An imprecise belief on X is a nonempty closed convex subset of ∆X. □X is the space of imprecise beliefs on a space X. µ, ν are used for probability distributions, and Ψ, Φ are used for imprecise beliefs. Expectations of functions with respect to imprecise beliefs are defined to be the worst-case expectation.
